To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MoxX, the labile antitoxic protein of B. anthracic toxin-antitoxic module, is a modular protein that contains a RHH domain, and that this domain is responsible for its autoregulatory function.
the MoxX toxin–antitoxin system has a modular structure and functions as a repressor of its own gene expression.
MoxT and MoxX form a toxin–antitoxin system and the MoxX is a DNA binding protein that regulates its own expression by binding to its upstream regulatory region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the structure and function of the B. antracis toxin-antioxin module MoxXT, and its role in regulation of toxin expression.
the identification of novel antibacterial targets and development of novel molecules for the same.
the molecular basis of the interaction between the toxin and antitoxin of B. anthracisis, which will provide insights into the structure and function of toxin–antitoxin systems in general.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MoxX has a modular structure with its N- and C-termini having distinct functions.
our study has provided a detailed understanding of the structure and function of the antitoxin MoxX and its interactions with MoxT.

we have modeled the structure of the B. anthracis MoxX antitoxin protein in its biologically relevant dimeric state and have identified the regions involved in its interactions with MoxT toxin and its own upstream DNA, which is essential for its autoregulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have modeled the structure of the antitoxin protein, MoxX and have identified the regions that are involved in the binding of MoxX to MoxT and to its own upstream regulatory DNA sequence.
MoxXT is a two component toxin–antitoxin system wherein MoxT is an endoribonuclease and MoxX is a DNA-binding repressor protein that mediates negative autoregulation of its own transcription.
we have modeled the structure of B. anthracisis MoxX and MoxXT complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MoxX, a small DNA-binding protein, can be used as a model system for understanding the molecular mechanisms of toxin-antitoxic interactions and DNA binding.
we have identified the structure of the antitoxin MoxX, its interactions with the toxin MoxT and with DNA, which can be exploited to design novel antibacterials.
the structure of MoxX can be exploited for design of molecules capable of disrupting its interactions with both its toxin and DNA.
